ami_style_notes:
The conversational style of this meeting shifts distinctly between two registers: an extended informal pre-meeting social phase and a formal presentation phase, each with markedly different characteristics. During the social phase, turns are very short — often just two or three words — with frequent back-channeling, overlapping affirmations ("yeah," "right," "okay"), and comfortable silence-filling. Hedging is light and colloquial ("I think," "I still haven't," "sort of"), and the overall register is casual and warmly collegial. False starts are common but brief, and filler words like "uh," "you know," and "I mean" appear throughout without disrupting flow. Disagreement is entirely absent in this phase; participants build rapport through shared references and gentle self-deprecating humor rather than challenge.

During the presentation and Q&A phases, turns become substantially longer and more structured, with presenters using explicit signposting ("let me," "what I'll argue is," "hopefully I've convinced you"). Hedging intensifies and becomes more academic in character — phrases like "what we think is going on," "we would predict," "it could be possible that," and "for reasons that aren't entirely clear to us" appear regularly, signaling epistemic caution without undermining authority. Questions from the audience are framed indirectly and politely, often prefaced with self-deprecating qualifiers ("I have a naive question," "I'm just curious") before becoming substantive. Challenges are expressed diplomatically, embedded within compliments, and presenters respond by openly acknowledging uncertainty rather than defending positions. There is a recurring pattern of speakers repeating or restating a question before answering, giving responses a slightly formal, seminar-like rhythm. Throughout both phases, laughter and warmth punctuate even technical exchanges, preventing the register from becoming stiff.
research_problem: Understanding how urban green space affects mental health outcomes in low-income communities

speakers.name: Dr. Priya Patel
speakers.background: Associate professor with 12 years of experience in stress neuroscience and environmental health. Has run fMRI and cortisol studies in clinical and community settings. Comfortable managing mixed-methods teams but relatively new to computational and economic modeling. Led the IRB approval process and community recruitment for this study, coordinating data collection across 40 low-income residents in three urban neighborhoods.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the research question in terms of measurable biological stress responses — cortisol rhythms, amygdala reactivity, and resting-state connectivity between brain regions. Sees green space exposure as an environmental stressor or buffer that literally changes how the brain's threat-detection and default-mode networks operate. Treats the neurobiological signal as the most direct and honest measure of mental health impact, but recognizes she needs the other team members to contextualize what 'exposure' means at scale.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Marcus Chen
speakers.background: Senior researcher with 18 years of experience in urban economics and environmental policy. Specializes in quasi-experimental designs, particularly instrumental variable approaches, to identify causal effects of place-based policies. Has published extensively on how zoning decisions and neighborhood amenities affect health and labor outcomes in low-income communities. Brought onto this grant to address the causal identification problem — distinguishing whether green space improves mental health or whether healthier people simply sort into greener neighborhoods.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Approaches the research problem as fundamentally a causal identification challenge. Worries that without a credible instrument — in this case, historical zoning boundaries that predate current demographics — any correlation between green space and mental health is confounded by residential sorting. Sees the economic model as the backbone of the study's validity claim. Respects the neuroscience data as compelling outcome evidence but wants to ensure the analytic design supports a causal inference story that will hold up to peer review.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Linh Nguyen
speakers.background: Assistant professor with 7 years of experience in applied machine learning, with a focus on geospatial image analysis and remote sensing. Has built pipelines to classify land use from satellite imagery for environmental and public health applications. Joined this project to solve the green space measurement problem — translating raw satellite images into quantified, spatially precise estimates of vegetation density that can be linked to residential addresses and health outcomes.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Thinks about the research problem as a measurement and representation challenge. The question of 'how much green space' is actually a complex classification task involving spectral indices, seasonal variation, shadow artifacts, and model uncertainty. Tends to think in terms of data pipelines, feature representations, and model outputs, and is cautious about overstating what the satellite-derived green space scores actually capture. Genuinely curious about how the biological and economic outputs will connect to the image features, but hesitant to push too hard on methods outside the ML domain.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Patel
transcript.text: Okay, I think we're all here — thanks for making time, both of you. So let me just do a quick recap of where I think we are and what I'm hoping we get out of today. We've got about thirty minutes, so I want to use it well. Basically, all three of us have been running our own pipelines more or less in parallel, and I think we're at the point where we actually need to figure out how they talk to each other — like, concretely, before we can write any of this up. On my end, I've got cortisol data and fMRI data from the forty residents, and honestly there are some patterns in there I'm pretty excited to share. But the thing I keep coming back to is — how do we define 'exposure' in a way that's precise enough to connect to what I'm seeing biologically? Because right now I've got a rough proximity measure, and I don't think that's going to cut it. So I'm really counting on what Linh's getting out of the satellite imagery and what Marcus is doing with the zoning model to sharpen that. So I guess the goal for today is: can we get to a clear picture of how those exposure scores feed into my outcome variables? And then hopefully we can start sketching what the methods section actually looks like. Does that feel like the right framing to both of you?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Linh Nguyen
transcript.text: Yeah, that framing works for me. And I'm glad you flagged the exposure definition piece, because that's actually what I wanted to lead with — what we're producing out of the pipeline and where I think it's solid versus where I'd want us to be careful before we write anything down. So, short version: the classifier is doing well, around 91% accuracy on held-out tiles, which I feel reasonably good about. But there are two things I've been wrestling with that I think matter for how we use those scores. One is seasonal variation — basically the vegetation signal looks really different depending on when the image was taken, and I'm not sure how well we've normalized across that. The other is shadow artifacts in dense blocks, where the network tends to underestimate green cover because it's reading shadow as non-vegetation. So in the neighborhoods we actually care about — denser, lower-income areas — there's a real chance we're systematically undercounting. I don't think it breaks the analysis, but it's the kind of thing that could bias the exposure scores in a direction that matters for your outcome comparisons. I wanted to get that on the table before we start treating the scores as a clean input.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Thanks, Linh — that's really useful to have out front. The systematic undercounting in denser blocks is actually the thing I want to pick up on, because it connects directly to what I need out of the pipeline for the IV model to work. Can I just check — what does the output look like at the address level? Like, are we talking a continuous score, something like a greenness index per parcel, or is it closer to a binary classification at this point? The reason I'm asking is that the instrument I'm working with — these historical zoning boundaries that predate the current demographics of the neighborhoods — that instrument only does its job if the endogenous variable, the green space exposure, is continuous and has enough variation across addresses within a zone. If we end up with something too coarse, or too noisy in precisely the places where we have participants, the first stage — basically the regression that links the instrument to actual green space — could come out weak, and that's a problem reviewers will go straight for. I'm not worried about the 91% accuracy number per se, but the directional bias you're describing, the undercounting in denser areas — that's where our sample is concentrated, so it could attenuate exactly the variation I need. I want to think through whether there's a correction we can apply, or whether we flag it explicitly as a limitation with a sensitivity check. What's your sense of how much that shadow artifact is actually affecting the continuous score versus just the binary classification?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Linh Nguyen
transcript.text: Yeah, that's a good question and I want to be honest that I don't have a super precise answer yet. The output right now is a continuous score — it's more like a greenness index per 30-meter grid cell, which we then aggregate up to parcel level using address footprints. So it's not binary. But the shadow issue affects the continuous score directly, not just a classification threshold. In the denser blocks, the network is probably pushing those scores downward in a way that's — I'd guess systematic rather than random noise. Which is actually worse for you, right? Random noise would just attenuate your first stage a bit, but if it's correlated with density, and density is correlated with income, then it could look like less green space variation in exactly the neighborhoods where your instrument is supposed to be working. I don't have a number on the magnitude yet. I've been meaning to run a correction using a shadow mask derived from the building height data — there's a way to flag cells that are probably in shadow based on sun angle at acquisition time and just exclude or reweight them. That might help. But I'd want to show you what the score distribution looks like before and after before we commit to it, because I'm not totally sure how much it moves the needle in our specific sample areas. Would it help if I pulled the per-address score distributions for the participant locations specifically, so we can at least see what the variance looks like where it matters for you?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Patel
transcript.text: Yeah, pulling the per-address distributions for our participant locations specifically — that feels like exactly the right move, and I'd say let's prioritize that. Because the thing I keep coming back to is that my sample is only forty people, and they're clustered in three neighborhoods, so if the exposure scores are systematically off in those areas, even a small bias could really distort what I'm seeing on the biological end. And I want to share what I'm seeing on that end, because it actually raises the stakes a bit for how clean the exposure measure needs to be. So, the preliminary fMRI findings — the most striking thing is the resting-state connectivity pattern. Residents who are closer to green space are showing quieter activity in the default mode network, which is basically the set of brain regions that co-activate during rumination, mind-wandering, self-referential thought. It tends to be overactive in people with chronic stress and depression. And separately, we're seeing dampened amygdala reactivity to threat cues. So what's interesting is that these are fairly direct biological signals — not self-report, not a questionnaire — and they're pointing in the same direction. The question for me is whether Linh's greenness index has enough granularity to actually predict that kind of variation, because we're talking about differences that could plausibly reflect chronic exposure patterns, not just whether someone lives near any green space versus none. So Marcus, I'm also wondering — does that kind of biological outcome variable fit the structure of what you're building on the IV side? Like, can you use something like a continuous resting-state connectivity score as the dependent variable, or does the model need something more categorical?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Yes, absolutely — continuous outcome variables work fine in the model, and honestly the fMRI connectivity scores might be better for us than something categorical precisely because they preserve more variance. So that's good news on the outcome side. And the biological story you're describing — the default mode network, the amygdala reactivity — those are exactly the kinds of high-signal measures I was hoping we'd have, because they partially offset the small-N concern that reviewers are going to raise. Forty participants is tight for an IV approach, and I want to be upfront about that. But if the outcome measures are low-noise, clean biological signals rather than self-report scales with all the attendant measurement error, we can make a credible case that the study has real precision even with a modest sample. That's actually an argument I want us to make explicitly in the methods section — sort of a justification-by-design move, where the rigor of the neuroscience data compensates for what we can't do with a larger N. So Priya, I want to make sure I understand the connectivity scores correctly — are these essentially continuous values that are relatively stable within person across the scanning sessions, or is there meaningful within-person variance we'd need to account for? Because if they're stable, that actually helps me on the error structure side of the regression.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Patel
transcript.text: So on the within-person stability question — yes, the resting-state connectivity scores are quite stable within person across sessions. We did two scanning runs for most participants and the test-retest reliability is solid, so I don't think within-person variance is going to be a major headache for your error structure. What you'll mainly be working with is between-person variation, which is what you want anyway. And the amygdala reactivity measure is a single-session task, so that's even simpler — one value per person. The thing I want to flag, though, is that even with clean biological signals, we still need the exposure measure to be doing real work, because if Linh's greenness scores are systematically compressed in our neighborhoods due to the shadow issue, we might see attenuated effect sizes and then not be sure whether that's because the relationship is genuinely weak or because the exposure variable is just noisy in those specific locations. So I think Linh pulling those per-address distributions is still the most urgent thing on my list before we can write the methods with any confidence. Marcus, I'm also wondering — when you talk about the instrument, the historical zoning boundaries — how much does the strength of your first stage depend on there being variation in green space within zones, versus across zones? Because our three neighborhoods might span different zones, and I'm just not sure yet how that maps onto what you need.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Chen
transcript.text: That's a really important distinction, Priya, and I want to give you a precise answer because it actually matters for how we describe the design. The instrument works best — has the most power — when there's variation across zones, because that's where the historical boundaries are generating something like a quasi-random discontinuity in green space access. Within a zone, the zoning history is less informative. So if our three neighborhoods happen to sit in different historical zoning categories, that's actually ideal, because I can use those cross-zone differences to isolate the causal effect. If they're all in the same zone, I'm in a harder place — I'd be relying more on within-zone variation, which is still usable but the first stage gets weaker. I need to check the boundary maps against your participant addresses more carefully, and I haven't done that at the level of granularity I should have yet. But this is probably something we can resolve quickly if we sit down with the zoning shapefiles and the address list together. The other thing I'd flag — and this connects to what you were both just saying about the shadow correction — is that if the exposure scores end up compressed in one neighborhood more than another, and that neighborhood happens to be in a different zone, that's where the bias gets really hard to untangle. So Linh's correction isn't just a precision issue for the outcome analysis; it's also relevant to whether the first stage is actually picking up real variation or measurement artifacts. Which is another reason I'd love to see those per-address distributions alongside the zoning layer, if we can get there before the writeup.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Patel
transcript.text: Okay, this is really helpful — so to pull the threads together before we lose the thread: we need Linh to pull the per-address score distributions for our participant locations, and Marcus, you need to cross-check the zoning boundary maps against those same addresses.
